lead: From today the first reading is the Book of Exodus. The family that Joseph saved is now a people, and “a new king arose over Egypt, who did not know Joseph.” Gratitude is forgotten, and a fear of the foreigner turns into slavery and the killing of newborn boys. In the Gospel Jesus closes the mission discourse of Matthew 10 with words that are hard to hear: he has not come to bring peace but a sword, and whoever loves father or mother more than him is not worthy of him. Yet the discourse ends with a promise: whoever welcomes the disciples welcomes Christ, and even a cup of cold water given to a disciple will not lose its reward. Psalm 124 holds the two readings together: “Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

r.h: A new king who did not know Joseph
set: The Book of Exodus takes its Greek name from the departure (exodos) of Israel from Egypt; in Hebrew it is called by its opening words, “These are the names”. It opens with a list of the sons of Jacob who came into Egypt (1:1–5), and a first note of fulfilment: “the Israelites were fruitful and prolific; they multiplied and grew exceedingly strong” (1:7). The language recalls the blessing of the creation of humankind (Genesis 1:28) and the promise to Abraham.

Background. The king is not named. Many scholars place the oppression in the thirteenth century before Christ, under the Pharaohs of the Nineteenth Dynasty, since the store cities Pithom and Rameses are in the eastern Delta; the Bible gives no name, and the date is debated. The text keeps its focus on the theme: a power that forgets the good done to it and fears the people who live in its land. The reading skips the story of the midwives Shiphrah and Puah, who refuse to kill the boys (1:15–21).
str: vv. 8–10: a new king who does not know Joseph fears the growth of the Israelites and proposes to “deal shrewdly” with them.
vv. 11–14: taskmasters, forced labour, store cities, bitter lives; yet the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied.
v. 22: Pharaoh commands that every Hebrew boy be thrown into the Nile.
kw: In the Bible “to know” means more than to have heard of: to recognize, to acknowledge. The king did not acknowledge what Joseph had done, and so did not recognize the people’s place in his kingdom.
The word for the forced labour in vv. 13–14 is the same word used later for the worship of God. The question of Exodus is: whom shall Israel serve? Pharaoh, or the Lord (Exodus 4:23)?
“They made their lives bitter” (v. 14). The memory is kept in the Passover meal, where bitter herbs are eaten as a sign of the bitterness of slavery.
vv: Now a new king arose over Egypt, who did not know Joseph.
Chapter 1 stands in contrast with the end of Genesis. There, Pharaoh honoured Joseph; here, the memory of the benefactor is lost. Gratitude can be forgotten within a generation.
Come, let us deal shrewdly with them,
The new policy is presented as prudence. Fear is turned into a plan that treats a whole people as a danger. The Bible uses the account to show how oppression begins in fear and calculation.
But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and spread,
The blessing of God cannot be stopped by oppression. It is the first sign in Exodus that the Lord is at work behind the scene.
and made their lives bitter with hard service in mortar and brick and in every kind of field labor.
The picture of bricks and mortar is well known from Egyptian paintings and texts. For Israel it is the memory of the house of bondage.
Every boy that is born to the Hebrews you shall throw into the Nile, but you shall let every girl live.
From forced labour the king moves to the killing of children. The Church’s memory of the slaughter of the innocents at Bethlehem (Matthew 2:16) hears an echo of this verse.
ch: The Church reads the Exodus as the great foundation of Israel’s faith, first of all the story of the Jewish people’s liberation, which Jews remember each year at Passover; Christians read it as the first stage of the history that leads to Christ. The Fathers saw in the slavery of Egypt a figure of the slavery of sin, and in the crossing of the sea a figure of Baptism. The Catechism recalls this in the liturgy of Baptism (CCC 1221). The slaughter of the boys, and the Child who is saved, prepare the reader for Moses, and for Jesus, who like him was saved from a king’s decree (Matthew 2:13–15). The Catechism also teaches that the seventh commandment forbids every enterprise that leads to the enslavement of human beings (CCC 2414). Today the Church prays for those who are held in forced labour or trafficked in many lands, and for those who do such wrong.

set: These are the last verses of the mission discourse. After the warning of persecution (10:16–23) and the call not to fear (10:24–33), Jesus now speaks of the cost within the household. The verses alternate between warning and promise. The discourse closes in 11:1 with the formula Matthew uses at the end of each of the five great discourses: “when Jesus had finished…”.

Background. The sword is a figure of division, as the parallel in Luke makes clear (12:51: “No, I tell you, but rather division”). Jesus is not calling for violence; he forbids Peter to use the sword in the garden (26:52). The words of vv. 35–36 come from the prophet Micah (7:6), who spoke of the breakdown of trust in a time of trouble. Jesus says that the call to follow him will split even families, as it did in the early Church, where a convert could be rejected by his house.
str: vv. 34–36: Jesus has come not to bring peace but a sword, to divide even members of one household.
vv. 37–39: whoever loves father, mother, son or daughter more than Jesus is not worthy of him; take up the cross; lose your life to find it.
vv. 40–42: whoever welcomes the disciples welcomes Jesus and the Father who sent him; the reward of the prophet, the righteous and the cup of cold water.
11:1: when Jesus had finished instructing the Twelve, he went on to teach in their cities.
kw: The short sword of the soldier or the knife of the sacrificer. As used here, it is a figure for division and decision, not for war.

This is the first mention of the cross in Matthew, long before the Passion. For his hearers it was the Roman punishment of the condemned, who carried the beam to the place of execution. The disciple is asked to follow the Master on the same road.
The word means life, soul and self. To “find” one’s life by clinging to it is to lose it; to give it up for Christ is to receive it back from God.
vv: Do not think that I have come to bring peace to the earth; I have not come to bring peace, but a sword.
The Christ whom the angels announced as bringing peace on earth (Luke 2:14) says that peace which avoids the truth is not what he brings. Following him divides, because it demands a choice.
and one’s foes will be members of one’s own household.
Taken from Micah 7:6. For first-century disciples, faith in Jesus could cost them the favour of their families. The verse describes a pain that the Church has seen in every age.
Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me;
Not a denial of family love, which God commands (Matthew 15:4–6), but the order of love: Christ first, and every other love in him.
and whoever does not take up the cross and follow me is not worthy of me.
The cross is not a general name for any trouble; it is the path of following Jesus, even to the point of giving up one’s life.
Those who find their life will lose it, and those who lose their life for my sake will find it.
A saying found in every Gospel. Life is a gift that is kept by being given, and lost by being clutched.
Whoever welcomes you welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me.
The chain of sending: Father, Son, apostles, and those who receive them. To welcome a messenger of Christ is to welcome God.
whoever gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones in the name of a disciple
The smallest act of kindness, given for Christ’s sake, has its reward. In Palestine, a cup of cold water was a precious courtesy in the heat.
ch: The Catechism, speaking of the fourth commandment, teaches that the bonds of family, though important, are not absolute: the call of Christ takes precedence, as Jesus says in v. 37 (CCC 2232). It teaches too that the way of perfection passes by way of the Cross, and that there is no holiness without renunciation and spiritual battle (CCC 2015). The saints are those who took these words literally, and found that the love of Christ makes love of family deeper, not smaller. The closing verses on welcome underlie the Church’s works of mercy, and the promise that a cup of water will not lose its reward is the “small way” of every Christian. The Church also prays for families divided over faith, that the peace of Christ may reach them.

qa: How can Jesus say he came to bring a sword when he is the Prince of Peace?

He speaks of the division that his call causes, not of violence. The peace he gives is real, but it is a peace that does not come by ignoring the truth or the demands of discipleship. Matthew puts these words beside Jesus’ refusal of the sword in Gethsemane (26:52). The Church does not read this verse as a justification for violence in the name of Christ, and she reminds us that the first to bear the cost of discipleship are the disciples themselves.
study: Where does following Jesus ask me to put him before something or someone I love, and how can this make my love of them deeper?
Who is “one of these little ones” to whom I can give a cup of cold water today, in the name of Christ?
